models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods move as gifts which create obligations to give and to return, so a maker builds standing and trust by sharing works freely and receiving acknowledgement in return. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that gifts create obligations, so works circulate among kin and allies, and makers outside those networks gain no reward and no say over who copies their work. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift; Sahlins, Stone Age Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a household balances its work against its needs, so a maker may share a work freely with neighbours, since the aim is use rather than sale. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that output serves consumption rather than sale, so a household that does not sell its works earns nothing from them, and others may copy them without paying the maker. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a central authority stores what it collects, so works and records are kept in public stores where they survive and can be consulted. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the centre allocates what it stores by rank, so creators close to officials win commissions and copying rights, while other makers go unrewarded and their works are shared only as the centre chooses. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation; Polanyi, Arensberg and Pearson, Trade and Market in the Early Empires

models.best: Inferred from its principle that output is sold through trade, so a finished work can be sold at once and its owner keeps a clear record of each sale. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour is extracted through the ownership of people, so enslaved makers are denied education and any right to their own works, and their writing, music or craft is taken and sold by owners. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a lord gives protection and justice in return for service, so a maker on the manor holds a secure place under local custom, and works made there are protected in the lord's court. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour and rents are owed to a lord, so the output of a bound maker belongs to the lord, and a writer or artist on the manor may not sell or copy a work without the lord's leave. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society; Capitulare de villis

models.best: The Statute of Anne (first copyright act) is reported to set fixed terms in statute: fourteen years for a new book, a second fourteen-year term for a living author, and 21 years for books already printed. The terms are unconfirmed, as the entry was not read in full, and a blog post in the results argues that the act aimed at the book trade's manufacturing side, not creative content.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that masters control entry and statutes fix training, so new makers wait for a place in the trade, and a closed body decides who may publish and copy. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Boileau, Le Livre des métiers; Epstein, Freedom and Growth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state aims for a surplus of gold and trade, so rules on copying are shaped to favour home makers and sellers whose trade brings in wealth. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The Statute of Anne (first copyright act) is reported to set fixed terms for books. A U.S. Intellectual History blog post argues that it aimed at the manufacturing side of the book trade rather than creative content. Inferred from its principle that the state regulates production for a trade surplus, producers may be served ahead of authors. The entry was not read in full, so the terms and that reading are unconfirmed. Source: History of Information online entry on the Statute of Anne, The First Copyright Statute (year not shown)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture creates a net product and that trade should be free, so books on farming and estate management circulate without monopoly grants on their copies. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture creates a net product, so writing, printing and the arts are treated as unproductive, and writers, artists and printers receive little support or legal protection for their works. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Quesnay, Tableau économique; Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy

models.best: A law review abstract reports that the Berne Convention (1886) sets national treatment, which gives foreign authors the same protection as local ones, and the abolition of formalities. The treaty text was not read, and the abstract's grouping of some provisions under 1886 is loose.
models.worst: Property protection can be lengthened by statute. The US Copyright Term Extension Act of 1998 lengthened US copyright by twenty years for existing and future works, as the Brookings-hosted copy frames it, and a 2002 brief by seventeen economists judged its gains very unlikely to exceed its costs, because the money from added years is worth almost nothing once discounted. The brief is one side's advocacy, not an empirical study, and an article in the Economics Working Paper Archive disputes its economics. Source: Brookings-hosted copy of a 2002 amicus brief by seventeen economists (Eldred v. Ashcroft)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, so the price a work earns in sales or licences shows what buyers value, and no planner sets it. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that state planning and credit expansion distort production, so state grants of exclusive rights and state commissions can steer which works are made away from what buyers want. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Menger, Grundsätze der Volkswirthschaftslehre; Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society

models.best: A law review abstract reports that the Berne Convention (1886) sets national treatment and the abolition of formalities. The treaty text was not read, and the abstract's grouping of some provisions under 1886 is loose.
models.worst: Copyright monopolies can be lengthened by statute. The US Copyright Term Extension Act of 1998 lengthened US copyright by twenty years, and a 2002 brief by seventeen economists judged its gains very unlikely to exceed its costs, citing monopoly losses and costlier derivative works. The brief is one side's advocacy, and an article in the Economics Working Paper Archive disputes its economics. Source: Brookings-hosted copy of a 2002 amicus brief by seventeen economists (Eldred v. Ashcroft)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public spending rises in slumps, so public commissions and grants for writers, musicians and artists rise when work is scarce, keeping them at their craft. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that spending falls in booms, so commissions and grants for creators are cut in strong years and widened only in slumps, and the supply of new works swings with the business cycle. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Keynes, The General Theory; Beveridge, Social Insurance and Allied Services

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a legal order curbs monopoly, so the rights in a work are limited in time and collecting bodies face competition, which keeps licence fees in check for users. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a legal order curbs monopoly, so if that order is weak, a few publishers or rights holders could hold most catalogues and set licence prices, while creators receive a small share of the proceeds. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Müller-Armack, Wirtschaftslenkung und Marktwirtschaft; Erhard, Wohlstand für Alle

models.best: Denmark's public lending right is a payment to authors for library lending, and a Canadian programme timeline credits Denmark with pioneering library compensation in 1946. That date rests on the timeline and a brief abstract, not on the Danish law, and no amounts or funding are given.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that universal public services are financed by high taxes, so public payments to creators may favour the most-borrowed authors, and new or niche works may wait for funds that the state allocates. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Saltsjöbaden Agreement; Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state directs support to chosen fields, so public money and copyright terms can help domestic makers in favoured fields, with support reviewed as those fields become competitive. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state picks the favoured fields, so makers in other fields get little public support, and support may continue for a field after it has stopped paying off. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle; Amsden, Asia's Next Giant

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the rent of land funds public services, so a levy on land value can pay for public libraries, archives and the arts, letting works reach the public without a sale price. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that land values carry the funding, so budgets for arts and archives rise and fall with land prices, and a downturn in land values cuts the support on which creators depend. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities built by example replace wage competition, so writers and artists form shared presses, theatres and archives, and share their works among members. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that communities are built by example, so a shared press or archive depends on its founders' vision and small budgets, and its works may be lost when the founders leave. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Owen, A New View of Society; Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit and free contracts let makers keep the full value of their work, so rents from exclusive rights are abolished and makers sell their works at cost. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit is lent at cost, so a maker who sells a work at cost earns little from it, and a shared fund must cover the costs of books and recordings that do not sell. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own and control their firms, one member one vote, with the surplus shared between users and workers, so authors and performers in a publishing co-operative share in the surplus. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that members own the firm and share its surplus, so a small or closed membership may run a publishing co-operative for insiders and leave newcomers and outside creators unpublished. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers; Mondragón cooperatives

models.best: A&M Records v. Napster concerned a peer-to-peer service that let users find and copy MP3 recordings stored on one another's computers, so copies moved directly between users, though the case entry is a summary, not the opinion, and its description of the service is unconfirmed against the entry.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no state and no contract, so no body can settle who made a work or enforce rules on copying, and disputes over sharing are left to goodwill alone. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' organisations run industry directly, so writers, performers and technicians set the terms of their work through their own bodies and win them by collective action. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that strikes are the main weapon, so a prolonged strike can halt the release of books, records or films and leave makers without income while the dispute runs. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Founding of the French CGT; Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail

models.best: Inferred from its principle that democratic, gradual reform builds public enterprise and a national minimum, so public libraries and archives, and a national minimum of support for writers and artists, are funded by the public. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that public enterprise changes gradually, so copyright terms and access are reformed in stages, each waiting on the last, and rules for works may stay out of date for long periods. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Fabian Essays in Socialism; Founding of the Fabian Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control through guild-like councils, so writers, performers and readers sit on councils that set the terms for works alongside the state. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that several councils share control, so no single body decides who holds rights, and decisions on licences and access stall between councils and the state. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry

models.best: Inferred from its principle that central plans set output and investment, so the state commissions the works it plans and pays makers from the plan, with the number of works in each field matched to planned needs. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state mobilises labour for planned goals, so works that do not fit the plan may not be published or copied, and makers may be sent to tasks the plan requires. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kornai, The Socialist System; First Five-Year Plan

models.best: Inferred from its principle that managers follow market prices, so a publicly owned publisher or studio prices its licences by market signals, while a central board sets the rules and the investment. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central board sets the rules and the investment, so rules for copying and reward may lag new kinds of work, and a slow board can leave creators waiting for decisions. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Lange and Taylor, On the Economic Theory of Socialism; Yugoslav workers' self-management

models.best: Inferred from its principle that once classes disappear, distribution follows need, so works are shared freely and makers receive according to need from a common store. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central authority judges ability and need, so it may decide who may publish and copy a work and whose needs count, leaving makers little choice over their own works. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership of key sectors works alongside markets, so public cultural bodies can license works at market terms, and special zones can pilot new rules for rights before wider use. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that price reform is gradual under party direction, so rules for rights and licences change in stages set from the centre, and protection may differ from region to region. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Naughton, The Chinese Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' and consumers' councils plan through repeated proposals, so creators and users decide which works are funded and shared, and the complexity of each job is balanced across people. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that repeated proposals and council votes decide what is funded or shared, so each round of planning takes time, and works may wait for decisions that arrive late. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions sit in state-controlled bodies, so creators and publishers are grouped into one body that collects fees for works and divides them among members. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Stagma, state-approved music-rights society in Germany, is reported to have held an extraordinary general meeting in Berlin in September 1933, following the society's monopolisation in Germany. The passage is short and sits in a secondary literary-history book, and it gives both 20 and 22 September for the meeting, so the date is unclear. Source: Austria Forum web book, an Austrian literary history in German (year not shown)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that interest is prohibited and finance shares profit and risk, so authors and publishers are financed by shared profit, and zakat can fund grants for makers who cannot pay. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that finance shares profit and risk, so an author's income rises and falls with each season's sales, and a failed book leaves the author as well as the publisher with a loss. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System; Founding of the Mit Ghamr savings bank

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic life serves well-being, so works are made in modest, local ways and shared within communities, and makers take only what a moderate living needs. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production is small-scale and local, so works that need large budgets, such as films or large print runs, are seldom made, and specialist makers must travel or go without. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Buddhist Economics; Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful

models.best: Inferred from its principle that property is widely held and enterprise is small, so many small presses, studios and craftsmen own their works and sell them directly, with a just wage for the makers. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that property is spread among many small owners, so a single work may have many small holders, each of whom must be asked before it is copied, which raises the cost of reuse. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum; Belloc, The Servile State

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic activity stays within planetary limits, so works are reused and shared rather than printed in ever larger runs, and a social floor gives every creator a basic living. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no growth imperative, so the market for new works is held back, and new creators find fewer places to publish or perform. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Daly, Steady-State Economics; Raworth, Doughnut Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every citizen receives an unconditional income, so authors and performers can write and perform without depending on sales, and works can be shared freely. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the income is paid for by taxes on land and natural resources, so a fixed sum paid to everyone may stay small, and makers who depend on royalties may find it does not replace their earnings from works. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Paine, Agrarian Justice; Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government issuing its own currency can fund full employment, so public money can pay for commissions, archives and public media, and inflation rather than debt sets the limit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation is the real limit, so if public spending on culture outruns the supply of studios, venues and printing, the cost of making works rises. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a community sharing a resource governs it with rules it designs, monitors and enforces, so creators and users who share an archive or library write and enforce the rules for copying and credit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a community designs and enforces its own rules, so the rules may close access to outsiders, and shared collections may be run for members only, leaving others without use of the work. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons

compromise.summary: Creators hold rights from the moment a work is made, for a fixed and published term that is never extended for works already made. Libraries pay authors for lending, foreign authors are treated as local ones, and more than one licensing body may operate. An independent review reports every year on output, licence fees and creators' income.
compromise.details: Keeps: fixed, published terms set in statute (Guild economy; Statute of Anne (first copyright act), terms unconfirmed); payment to authors for library lending, with no amounts given (Nordic social democracy; Denmark's public lending right); equal treatment of foreign authors (Classical laissez-faire capitalism and Monetarist neoliberalism; Berne Convention (1886), treaty text not read). Blocks: term extensions for existing works, by applying new terms only to new works after a published cost review (Monetarist neoliberalism; US Copyright Term Extension Act of 1998); one state-approved licensing body, by requiring more than one body with open membership (Corporatism and fascist economics; Stagma, state-approved music-rights society in Germany). Test: yearly counts of new works published and licensed, licence fees and payments to creators, over a period fixed in statute before any change. Source: History of Information online entry on the Statute of Anne; Canadian public lending right history timeline; University of Michigan law review abstract; Brookings-hosted copy of a 2002 amicus brief (Eldred v. Ashcroft); Austria Forum web book.
